# The Productivity Illusion: When Busyness Masks Misalignment

## Introduction

A workshop can look productive because everybody is busy. Machines hum, hands move, conversations overlap, and the sheer volume of activity suggests that progress must be happening. But appearances deceive. The people in that busy workshop may be solving entirely different problems—some may be solving the wrong problem altogether, and a few may not even be sure what problem they are supposed to be solving. Meanwhile, the person who pauses to ask a basic question can seem to slow things down, when in fact that question may be preventing several days of wasted work. The real challenge, then, is not simply keeping people busy. It is deciding when to interrupt the flow of activity and when to let an experiment finish. This essay explores that tension, though it must be said at the outset that no formula resolves it cleanly.

## The Seduction of Visible Activity

Busyness is easy to measure and easy to mistake for progress. A manager walking through a workshop sees sparks flying, saws cutting, and people carrying materials back and forth. Everything signals productivity. But activity and progress are not the same thing, and the gap between them can be enormous.
